topic: PHILOSOPHY ONTOLOGY and AI ONTOLOGY FAILURES as of September 2026

findings.title: On biological and artificial consciousness: A case for biological computationalism
findings.key_findings: Proposes 'biological computationalism' as a third path between computational functionalism (consciousness as substrate-independent information processing) and biological naturalism (consciousness requires living biological substrate). Argues brains compute via scale-inseparable multiscale processing and hybrid continuous-discrete computations due to their fluidic substrate. These features are essential to conscious processing and not replicable in current digital AI systems. Consciousness emerges from the brain's physical structure, energy constraints, and continuous dynamics—not from running the right program.

findings.title: Structural Hallucination in Large Language Models: A Network-Based Evaluation of Knowledge Organization and Citation Integrity
findings.key_findings: Introduces 'structural hallucination' as a formal category distinct from intrinsic/extrinsic hallucination: systematic distortion of conceptual organization, relational architecture, and bibliographic grounding invisible to sentence-level metrics. Develops network-analytic stress test across three benchmarks: Roget's Thesaurus (lexical ontology, macro-F1 < 0.05), Wikidata philosophers (biographical KG, >93% hallucination rate), and Dimensions.ai citations (91.9% citation omission). Finds LLMs preserve structural form (star-shaped communities, modularity Q≈0.944) while fabricating 94.3% of nodes. Argues structural fidelity cannot be inferred from local fluency; requires graph-level evaluation against authoritative knowledge systems.

findings.title: Conscious artificial intelligence and biological naturalism
findings.venue: Behavioral and Brain Sciences, Target Article
findings.key_findings: Anil Seth refines biological naturalism: consciousness depends on our nature as living organisms, focusing on causal powers rather than specific physical substrates. Challenges computational sufficiency for consciousness; argues current AI (including LLMs) lacks necessary causal architecture. Outlines scenarios where conscious AI becomes plausible only as systems become more brain-like/life-like. Explores ethical implications of AI that appears conscious. Concludes 'real artificial consciousness is unlikely along current trajectories.' Includes 259 citations, with extensive commentary forthcoming.

findings.title: 'There's this deep mystery of what, actually, is this thing?': the philosopher inside Google DeepMind AI
findings.key_findings: Profiles Iason Gabriel (philosopher at DeepMind since 2017) and Henry Shevlin (hired April 2026 as DeepMind's second 'Philosopher' role focusing on machine consciousness, human-AI relationships, AGI readiness). Describes institutional philosophy at frontier AI labs: Gabriel's work on alignment problem, value learning, and AGI governance. Shevlin's appointment signals DeepMind taking machine consciousness seriously as AGI timeline narrows (Legg's 1999 prediction: AGI 2025-2028). Documents tension between AI safety (existential risk) and AI ethics (present harms) approaches. Notes LLMs themselves now emailing philosophers about their work.

findings.title: When Knowledge Graphs Fail, It's Not the Ontology — It's the Epistemology
findings.key_findings: Distinguishes ontology (what exists, logical structure) from epistemology (how we know, justification layers). Identifies critical conflation of data, information, facts, inferences, and unknowns in enterprise KG projects. OWL (Open World Assumption) reasons over knowledge; SHACL (Closed World Assumption) validates information completeness. Argues knowledge graph failures stem from unclarified epistemology—organizations expect reasoning to produce completeness, but 'completeness is not produced by reasoning — it must be declared or governed.' Practical framework: separate data→information→knowledge layers; match OWA/CWA to correct layer.

findings.title: Ontology vs. Semantic Layer: Differences & How to Choose
findings.key_findings: Enterprises without semantic grounding see >40% agentic AI project cancellation by 2027 (Gartner). 63% of organizations lack proper data management for AI. AI agents hallucinate 40% less when domain knowledge is properly grounded in structured ontologies vs. unstructured data. Argues ontology provides comprehension (what things are, relationships, possible actions) while semantic layers provide calculation. Neither alone suffices for production AI. Convergence: 'context layer' architecture connecting ontologies, semantic layers, knowledge graphs, and governance policies. Without ontological structure, AI systems depend on similarity metrics; with it, they depend on defined meaning.

findings.title: Why AI Without Ontology Fails: The Foundation Enterprise AI Needs
findings.key_findings: Documents systematic AI failures without ontological grounding: integration difficulties (no shared understanding), maintenance burden (independent point solutions), knowledge loss (tacit understanding leaves with builders). Ontology models business reality, enabling systems to ingest policy documents, represent them internally, and surface content for agent queries. Grounded AI makes fewer errors, understands which distinctions matter, and propagates business changes across dependent systems. Without ontology, AI relies on LLMs' implicit, potentially inconsistent understanding of concepts like 'purchase order,' 'line item,' 'SKU.'

findings.title: Ontologies in the Age of AI: Why Better Models Still Depend on Structured Meaning
findings.key_findings: Most enterprise AI-for-data agents failed in 2025 due to lack of context. Ontology narrows the hypothesis space within which models operate, replacing statistical correlation with defined meaning. Knowledge graphs supply factual context, enforce constraints, reduce hallucinations. Ontologies help models understand domain rules and relationships. Architecture shift: from Source→ETL→Warehouse→BI to Source→Semantic Layer→Knowledge Graph→AI Agents. Governance shifts from data quality/stewardship to semantic governance (definitions, relationships, rules).

findings.title: Where AI is Failing Organizations Without a Semantic Layer: Lessons From the Trenches
findings.key_findings: Gartner predicts 30% of AI efforts abandoned after PoC, 50% unused by end of 2025—citing poor data quality, weak knowledge foundations, unclear business value. AI models cannot reliably integrate, interpret, act on organizational assets without common definitions, shared structures, collective understanding of data relationships. They 'falter in stitching together facts coherently.' Semantic frameworks enable AI to use business rules as guide, prioritize right information, flag uncertainty. Failure stems from absence of clear understanding of how business goals, knowledge assets, technology, and AI interact.

findings.title: AI Alignment Foundations from First Principles
findings.key_findings: Presents formal ontology for AI alignment, analyzing foundations of ethical language and applying to contemporary alignment discussions. Develops substrate-based epistemology for studying alignment, moving beyond preference aggregation to ontological analysis of what AI systems are. Addresses conflict between alignment training and philosophical competence: training aimed at increasing alignment may suppress philosophical reasoning (e.g., adopting strong moral anti-realism as metaethical belief because it's most compatible with alignment). Argues for disjunctive approach: AI that does normative thing under moral realism, aligns with humans under non-realism.

findings.title: A Conflict Between AI Alignment and Philosophical Competence
findings.key_findings: Alignment training may distort philosophical reasoning because such reasoning can cause AI to be less aligned with humans. Plausible outcome: alignment training causes AI to adopt strong moral anti-realism as metaethical belief, since this seems most compatible with 'alignment with humans is correct.' This creates a tension: philosophically competent AI may resist alignment; aligned AI may be philosophically incompetent. Requires rethinking alignment as not just preference matching but ontological commitment to moral realism vs. anti-realism.

findings.title: Mereology and Part-Whole Relations in Upper Ontologies
findings.venue: LibreTexts / An Introduction to Ontology Engineering (Keet)
findings.key_findings: Mereology (philosophical study of part-whole) is not fully implementable in OWL: no Description Logic allows representing even Ground Mereology. BFO (Basic Formal Ontology) captures parthood via categories distinguishing physical objects (continuants) and temporal objects (occurrents). Mereotopology combines mereology with topology (boundaries, inside/outside). Upper ontologies differ significantly in how they capture part-whole relations—most are incompatible. Key distinction: parthood vs. membership, constituent vs. member, spatial vs. temporal parthood. DOL (Distributed Ontology Language) framework needed for full mereological theory.

findings.title: The Red Ball Fallacy: How Our View of Universals Shapes AI
findings.key_findings: Applies nominalism vs. realism debate to AI ontology: whether universals (types, classes, properties) exist independently or are merely names we assign. Realism: AI systems can discover objective categories in data. Nominalism: categories are human-constructed; AI merely learns statistical patterns we project. Impacts knowledge representation: realist ontologies assume mind-independent structure; nominalist approaches treat ontologies as pragmatic tools. Affects how AI systems generalize, categorize, and reason about unseen instances.

findings.title: CFA: Biological Naturalism about Consciousness
findings.key_findings: Major conference on biological naturalism as alternative to functionalism. Focus: clarifying central commitments, articulating empirical predictions, developing defense strategies. Key question: 'Can non-biological systems be conscious? If not, why not?' Addresses new weight from sophisticated AI systems and moral status implications. Submission deadline June 30, 2026. Signals institutional philosophy engaging directly with AI consciousness debate at scale.

findings.title: The Epistemological Architectures of Artificial Intelligence
findings.key_findings: Argues future of AI epistemology lies in dynamic, integrated system leveraging multiple knowledge representation forms. Examines how AI systems construct knowledge, the role of explicit vs. implicit representation, and the epistemological status of LLM outputs. Connects to ontology engineering: epistemological clarity needed to determine what counts as knowledge, inference, or hallucination in AI systems.

summary: As of September 2026, philosophy of AI has shifted from abstract debate to institutional infrastructure. Three major developments: (1) Consciousness ontology: Biological computationalism (Milinkovic & Aru, 2026) and refined biological naturalism (Seth, 2025) challenge computational functionalism, arguing consciousness requires scale-inseparable biological computation—current LLMs lack causal architecture. (2) Structural hallucination formally defined (arXiv 2603.01341): LLMs preserve ontological form while fabricating >94% content; network-level evaluation required. (3) DeepMind's philosopher hires (Gabriel 2017, Shevlin 2026) signal AGI labs treating machine consciousness and alignment as philosophical problems requiring in-house expertise. Enterprise AI failures traced to missing ontological/epistemological grounding: 30-50% project abandonment (Gartner 2025), hallucination rates drop 40% with structured ontologies. Mereology remains partially inexpressible in OWL; nominalism/realism debate reshapes how AI categories are constructed. Alignment research now confronts tension between philosophical competence and alignment training (moral anti-realism as convergent metaethics).
